Hon. LUCIEN CANNON (Solicitor General) moved the second reading of Bill No. 313, to amend the Dominion Elections Act.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, as the house will recall, early in the ' session a special committee was appointed for the purpose of examining into the Elections Act and to recommend amendments which would improve the electoral system which now prevails in the Dominion. That committee has sat throughout the session, has held numerous meetings, heard a large number of witnesses, and has brought in a report attached to which is a draft bill containing the unanimous recommendations of the committee. I wish, Mr. Speaker, not only on behalf of the government but on behalf of the members of the house, to offer my hearty thanks to all the members of the committee for the work which they have performed, and for the unanimity of the decisions which they have reached. And may I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to make a special reference to the work done by the chairman of that committee, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power).
Dominion Elections Act

The legislation which is now introduced embodies the unanimous recommendations of the committee. I am ready to give any explanation on the bill that may be necessary when the clauses are considered in committee. May it suffice for me to state now that this legislation contains chiefly two new principles in our electoral system. The first concerns the appointment of the returning officers. Under the existing law returning officers were appointed by the governor in council upon the recommendation of the Secretary of State. There had been an attempt to give to the office of returning officer the character of permanency, but on account of the feeling which prevailed in the two leading parties in Canada, it has been the custom for the party in power to appoint the returning officers, and if that party did not happen to be returned to power the returning officers were dismissed and replaced by others. As a result, there has been among the members of the committee a feeling that this system ought to be altered, that the governor in council, that is the government or the party in power at the time of the issuing of the writs, or before, should no longer have the authority or the power to appoint the returning officers but that that authority and power should be vested in the chief electoral officer whose actions are surrounded by such safeguards as to guarantee his entire and complete independence in these matters. That is the first amendment, the first new principle introduced in this legislation, namely, the appointment by the chief electoral officer of all returning officers throughout the Dominion.
The second new principle introduced by this [DOT] legislation is that of the appointment of enumerators to prepare the election lists in urban centres. It appeared from what was said by members of the committee, and by witnesses who were heard before that committee, that in rural constituencies the present system of making up the lists has given, if not complete satisfaction, at least considerable satisfaction, and that only minor alterations will be necessary. On the other hand, in the large urban centres, the present system of making up the electoral lists is open to a great deal of criticism, and that for three reasons. The federal list which was made up for the purpose of the election was based on the provincial list then existing, if there was such a provincial list, and that as a result there were many inaccuracies in the Dominion list and the candidates had to go to considerable trouble and expense to check up that list; that the delays were very often prolonged, and that as a consequence of those

delays the lists were put in the hands of the candidates at a time so near the election date that they were practically useless. By this bill we do away altogether with provincial lists as a basis for the Dominion list, and the work of drawing up the list is assigned to officials, to be called enumerators, who will be appointed by the returning officers, and who will perform in the urban centres the work that at the present time is done in the rural constituencies by the enumerators.

In a large city, where there are many tenement houses and a large number of people resident in a polling division, sometimes it is difficult to get a proper scrutineer. Then my hon. friend's suggestion would foe that the clause read something like this: " Any voter qualified to vote in the electoral district for which the registrar has been appointed." Is that correct?
Yes.

Colonel Biggar has just
pointed out that the registrar is not likely to have before him the complete list of all the voters in the entire electoral district. In the ordinary course he will have before him the list of twelve polling subdivisions which comprise his registration district, but he will not have the complete list of all the electoral divisions, so it would be fairly difficult for him to check up in order to see whether or not the objector is a voter in that particular electoral division.

I think it would be quite
sufficient if an elector, coming before the registrar, made oath that he was a qualified voter. At least that would be presumptive evidence that he was a voter and he should be allowed to file an objection against a name on the list which properly should not be there. I think that should foe sufficient, because it is so difficult in some of the city
78594-192J
divisions where you are limited to the polling division to obtain the aid of those who are really qualified to examine into the qualifications of the voters on the list.

If the hon. member will
permit thi ssection to stand, we will insert the proper amendments afterwards.

Is any provision being
made for the man qualified to vote but who objects to being put on the list because the assessor might assess him the So poll tax? In Walkerville and Windsor we find many cases where single men avoid being placed on the list in order to escape the $5 poll tax.

There is no provision made for compulsory registration or voting, if that is what the hon. member means. Where a man's name is placed on the list by the enumerator he will have a pretty hard time to get it off unless he is willing to swear that he is not qualified to vote.
Schedule stands.
On section 16-Polling day.

Mr. Chairman, has an
endeavour been made to ascertain how many people are carried to the polls in any constituency and having neighbours vouch for their being residents of the district?

In rural polling divisions it is done- very generally, but I do not think any record is kept. The information could be obtained by looking at the poll books for the rural polling subdivisions throughout the country.

I suppose the Solicitor
General concurs with the chairman of the committee in stating that this practice is pretty general. I desire to state that it is not general, that very few people vote in that way. I believe that very simple factor prevented! the committee from considering a matter which, in my opinion is of supreme importance. We all believe in what might be called educated democracy; we believe that the people should be the jury which pronounces upon governments. As a matter of fact, what happens? In Canada 66 per cent of the people who. are entitled to vote go to the poles to register their vote, and of that 66 per cent, 33 per cent are carried to the polls by the energy and efforts of the political parties. One-third of the people of our country only are sufficiently concerned with the affairs of Canada to go to the polls and register a vote without being urged to do so. That condition is not peculiar to Canada; it obtains in a great many countries. We
Dominion Elections Act

have gone to a great deal o>f trouble to work out amendments to take care of matters which are insignificant as compared with this. Our efforts should be directed towards those who do not vote or who do not care to vote, just as is done in other countries.
In Australia, for instance, they had only 48 per cent of the people casting their votes in general elections; the percentage rose to 50 and the government of Australia began to recognize the fact that something should be done to induce the people to cast their votes without being carried to the polls. What was the result? In the two last general elections over 90 per cent of the people on the voters' lists went to the polls and voted. I am not saying that we in Canada should carry out the methods adopted in other countries, because that might be considered as compelling the people to vote. But what I do say is this: Something should be done with regard to the man who does not vote, and I consider that it is quite within the rights of the people who make the laws of the country to ask the jury to appear at the polls once in four years and pronounce upon the conduct of the government. It is surely not asking too much of a man to say that he should appear once in four years to register his vote. If there is a reason why he could not go to the polls, nothing should be done, but if there is no reason, measures should be taken to impress upon him the importance of casting his vote. The first and the simplest suggestion I have to offer is this:	That
man's name should not appear upon the voter's list for some little time. I would not say how long that time should be, but there is an absurdity in looking up these people every four years and going to the cost of preparing lists, putting the same people on those lists year after year, and election after election, and then having 30 per cent of them absenting themselves from the polls. Thirty per cent- of the cost is absolutely wasted. I would like to place upon Hansard a letter which I received from the Prime Minister of Australia, dated March 16, 1927, as follows: Dear Dr. Kaiser:
With reference to your letter of the 8th January, I have very much pleasure in forwarding you herewith copy of the Commonwealth Electoral Act 1918-25, and copy of the Electoral and Referendum Regulations, Statutory Rules 1926/201. I am also enclosing a graph which shows in respect of each eeetion and referendum held since the inception of the Commonwealth:

(a)	the number of electors enrolled;
(b)	the number of electors to whom ballot-papers were issued; and
(c)	the percentage of electors to whom ballot-papers were issued to electors enrolled.
(Mr. Kaiser.]
I cannot recall press criticism of any consequence against the introduction of compulsory voting. At the 1925 federal elections the government was returned to power with a very strong majority in the House of Representatives and it secured every vacant seat in the Senate. In the press after the elections there was much comment as to whether compulsory voting had been responsible for the government victory.	,
Some sections of the press took the view that the introduction of the compulsory voting did not affect the proportion of votes in favour of the government, while other sections claimed that it had materially assisted the government. The outstanding feature of the voting, however, was the large number of electors who recorded their vote, the percentage for the last election being 91 per cent. Prior to the introduction of the compulsory voting in 1917, the percentage of federal voters was 78.30 and in 1922 it fell to 59.36.
It is rather difficult to gauge the effect of the compulsory voting at the last federal election, as at the time owing to the activities of the communistic element in Australia there were many people who had previously voted for the Labour party but wbo did not do so on the last occasion.	.
I very much appreciate the remarks which you have so kindly made regarding my recent visit to Canada.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd) P. M. Bruce.
Those are the simple facts in connection with Australia. I would like to see similar ideas given currency in this country to the end that greater attention might be paid to the 66 per cent who either do not vote or who have to be carried to the polls, and less attention to the 33 per cent who voluntarily go to the polls.

In his opening
remarks, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Kaiser) stated that the committee had no knowledge that many people had their votes sworn in on election day. In my experience in western Canada, and I think in the experience of practically all the members from that section of the country, we find that in the rural districts many votes are sworn in on election day. Our enumerators have long distances to travel. Some people live in remote parts of the polling divisions and are missed in making up the electoral lists. The result is that on election day, in practically every poll in the rural districts of western Canada, a few are sworn in who are entitled to vote.

In answer to the last part of the remarks of the hon. member for Ontario, may I point out that it is a common thing in the rural districts to find from 75 to more than 90 per cent of the electors turning out on voting day. This is all a matter of whether the electors are interested in the election or not. If they are

Dominion Elections Act
not interested, no amount of law will make them vote. You could prosecute and go to a great deal of trouble in the matter and yet you could not force them to vote unless they were interested in doing so.

The hon. member for
Ontario put his views before the committee in a very interesting way, but the committee, after having considered the views as expressed by the hon. member, decided not to include them in their report. This legislation is along the lines of the unanimous report of the committee. I hope the hon. gentleman within a very short time will manage to have more converts on his side and then we shall introduce compulsory voting in Canada. This year, however, apparently the members who sat on the committee and considered the question, were not ready to go as far as the hon. gentleman was prepared to do.

The Solicitor General was
very courteous to me from the beginning of the discussion and I have no fault to find with him. All that I endeavoured to do was to begin casting a few seeds so that some day something along the lines I suggested might be done. There is no harm in doing that.

May I say a word or two with respect to subsection (2) which reads:
The day fixed for the poll shall at any election be a Monday, unless the Monday of the week in which it is desired to hold the poll
(a)	is a holiday as defined by the Interpretation Act; or
(b)	at a general election, is a day which is generally observed by the residents of any province as a day for religious exercises and is declared to be a holiday by the law of such province.
Why is it that those who drafted this section fixed Monday as a rigid, definite day upon which the election should be held? Perhaps it is because it so immediately follows Sunday that the electors come to the polls in a holy frame of mind.
And it is two days from Saturday.

That would make people of my persuasion half as religious on Monday as those who attend church on Sunday. A number of holidays, which are observed by the people of my persuasion, take place in the autumn of every year. If it were to happen that the election should fall on any one of those days, it might mean that I would disappear from the house at the next election and also my good friend the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. The latter would be a calamity frightful to contemplate.
For the hon. member.

It seems to me that this
clause ought, to stand over for further consideration. I am sure it is not the desire of any hon. member to have a law passed which would in any way interfere with the franchise of British citizens who hold religious views different from those of the majority. I am sure that is not the idea and there are people of my persuasion to be found in every electoral district in Canada. It is only right that I, as a member of that persuasion, should point out to the government the difficulty of adhering to a rule of this kind. There ought to be some flexibility. If it be found that Monday is a religious holiday observed by a number of people, it should be changed to Tuesday or some other day which would be agreeable.

The reason why the amendment was inserted was that it was represented by the chief electoral officer and by Colonel Biggar that, by having Monday as election day, it was more convenient to fix the dates upon which several different things were te be done by officials and so forth. I appreciate the argument brought forward by my hon. friend. He wishes the clause to stand. I might point out that subsection (2), as it reads now, states:
Unless the Monday of the week in which it is desired to hold the poll (a) is a holiday as defined by the Interpretation Act.
That would not apply.

That would not apply to holidays which are not included in the Interpretation Act. We might let the clause stand for the present and see if we cannot devise some way of meeting my hon. friend's wishes.
Section stands.
Sections 17, 18 and 19 agreed to.
On section 20-Name not on list.

We on this side have not
had an opportunity of looking at the bill. I just want to ask the minister whether it has been made clear in this section as to a voter casting his vote in the electoral district or in the polling division. For instance, the act specifically provides for a residence of two months in the electoral district. Then when the man comes to cast his vote, the instructions sent to the deputy returning officer read
Dominion Elections Act

"in the polling division" and not "in the electoral district" so that one contradicts the other. I brought the matter to the attention of the committee.

The idea which underlies this clause is as follows: In a- rural constituency, if a man found that his name was not on the list, he could, by taking the appropriate oath, register his vote, whereas the same privilege does not exist in the cities. But the returning officers were prone to interpret the act as meaning that if a man's name were not on the list, he was deprived of his vote. This amendment is inserted in order to make the matter very clear that if a man has his name on the list he is entitled to vote at the appropriate polling station, and in order to make the distinction very clear as between rural and urban polling divisions.

I understand that. My question is whether the act has been changed so as to make it specific whether the qualifications call for a residence of two months in the electoral district or in the polling division.

The oath has been changed to suit the wishes of my hon. friend. I remember well that he made certain representations to the committee with regard to the oath to be taken by people in rural polling divisions, and I think the oath has been changed to suit his views.
To be quite clear on that, do I understand from the answer that has been given, that the principle has not been changed, but that it has been made a little more specific?

Exactly. At the present time in order to vote under those circumstanices the applicant for a vote must take the whole oath. He is not allowed to swear as he did before simply that he resides in the electoral division. He must take the whole oath, that ihe has resided in the division for two months,
a British subject, and so forth.

Section agreed to.
On section 21-Advance polls.

I have not had time to read this section carefully, Ibut I would point out that there has been a great deal of misunderstanding in the rural constituencies in regard to advance polls. If the chief electoral officer is advised that there is a certain number of railway men, commercial travellers and others who want to vote at an advance poll he will establish an advance poll for that

town. It may be a town of three or five thousand people. The question did arise where there was an advance poll in one town and commercial travellers, railway men and railway mail clerks went to the returning officer of their own municipality and asked him for a certificate to allow them to go over to the neighbouring town and vote at the advance poll there. I can understand that in any city constituency there .might be trouble about it, but there would be very little trouble in a rural constituency where everyone knows everyone else, and it would seem to me to be well that in a village or town where there are commercial travellers, railway men or railway mail clerks, they should receive a certificate from the deputy returning officer of their polling division allowing them to drive over to the neighbouring town and vote at the advance poll there. There was a difference of opinion about this question in our by-election, the Conservative lawyers holding that the men could go over and vote, and the Liberal lawyers holding that they could not. I should like the Solicitor General to make the point clear.
Under the law at that time the Liberal lawyers were right.
If my hon. friend will read subsection 2A of section 21 he will see that it provides for the case he mentions.

I take it, then, from the Solicitor General that a railway mail clerk, a commercial traveller or any of the classes I mentioned, has a right to drive over to a neighbouring town where there is an advance poll being held and vote in that constituency.

Yes, if the chief electoral officer so directs. The chief electoral officer may direct that an advance poll may be used for a certain area, not only for the place where it is situated but for adjoining sections.
He may so direct, but would it take in the entire rural constituency? It would be necessary to secure his ruling in the matter prior to election day.

Yes, but under this law the returning officers will be made permanent officers, and they will organize their constituencies and be in a position to make all these arrangements with the chief electoral officer in advance, so I think the needs of the situation mentioned by my hon. friend will be met.

Section agreed to.

Dominion Elections Act
On section 22-When polls to be open.

Instead of having the
hours from two to ten o'clock on Saturday would it not be better to fix an earlier hour? What objection would there be to having it from eight o'clock on the day immediately preceding the voting day, because circumstances might arise which would make it advisable for citizens to vote in the morning.

The answer is to be found
in the note. This matter was discussed in the committee. The note says:
The proposed extension of hours on Saturday is thought likely to meet the necessities of the situation without compelling the election officers and candidates' agents who serve at advance polls to give up their regular employment for the purpose.
One of the reasons why voting day was fixed for Monday was that then theTe would be the whole afternoon of Saturday as well as Thursday evening and Friday evening for the advance polls. If it came in the middle of the week it would mean withdrawing from their regular occupation the number of people usual to man the polls. The same objection arises with regard to Saturday morning. It is a matter of convenience for the candidates and the electoral officials and for the public generally.

Does not the hon. member think that any inconvenience to the candidates and electoral officials would be outweighed by the convenience to the public at large being able to yote on Saturday morning while in town on their business, and then they could have the whole of Saturday afternoon free.
These are advance polls for people who have no business in the towns- commercial travellers, railway men, mariners and so forth,
But they may want to go away.

Is it provided in this
bill that newly naturalized citizens will have to have their naturalization papers with them in order to vote?

There is nothing in the
law about that.
The law should provide for that because in my home town I have known fifty people to vote on the same naturalization paper who were not entitled to vote at all.

If he takes the oath it
is not necessary for him to show his naturalization papers.

In this country a great
many newly arrived people are easily made the tools of other interested people. I know for a fact that interested! people, knowing that these newly arrived do not appreciate the value of their naturalization papers, will use them for fifty other people who are not entitled to vote.

That is somewhat in line
with the suggestion frequently made that people who register at hotels should carry their marriage certificate with them. If we were to insert any clause of that sort in the act every person who went to the polls would have to produce his birth certificate or his naturalization certificate. It was felt that when we provided that people could be sworn as to their qualifications we were going as far as we could go.

And there is always the
penalty for perjury.
Yes.

In some sections of
Europe they have to bring their papers to be allowed to vote.
Not under the law.

There is an anomaly
there. A good many people with the best intentions are voting when they are not entitled to vote. I have a good many of them in my section, and some interested people make it a point to see that these.people who are not entitled to vote do vote.
Swear every one of them.

There are a good many
people who vote that way, but I do not agree with my friend that they do it with the best intentions.

If the suggestion of the
hon. member were earned out it would prevent hundreds of legitimate voters from voting on election day. I have seen cases myself, of men who have been in this country for twenty or thirty years who have been precluded from voting on election day; their names were on the list but the returning officer positively refused to allow them to vote, and I am glad to have the 'assurance of the Solicitor General that these people will now be allowed to vote. As I say, I have known hundreds of men and women who have been in this country for many long years being sent out of a polling booth on election day because they did not have their certificates with them; they were told to go and fetch them, but they went out of the polling booth
Dominion Elections Act

anad never bothered to return. It should be the duty of the returning officer to see whether these men and women are naturalized or not. If he is not satisfied that a man or a woman is a Canadian citizen he should siwear them, and if he feels then after they have been properly sworn that everything is in order they should be allowed to vote.

In our section of the country practically one-fifth of the people are not on the list; there are many people up there whose votes were taken away from them in the manner mentioned by the hon. member, but that statement does not do away wilbh the fact that hundreds, yes, thousands of people are voting and who are certainly not entitled to vote.

Section agreed to.
Sections 23 and 24 agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, if hon. gentlemen will turn to page 29, there is a schedule which includes the constituencies where the fifteen-day system will exist instead of the eight-day system which is general throughout the Dominion. It has been generally agreed that this schedule 3 might stand, and any member of the house who wishes to have the name of his constituency included might so inform the officers of the house.
What page is that?
Page 28.

speechtext:
There are a number of other sections before we reach that.
Section 25 agreed to.
On section 27

Two weeks interval between nomination and polling days.
This is under section 27, as to the names of the constituencies-
Let us pass this act up to the point-
The said act is amended by adding to schedule 3 thereof-
We have had form 35. We have not yet passed form 36 following.

No. We are at section
27 now, page 28.
Yes, that is done.
Well, I have been listening and I did not hear the forms.
We are at 27 now.
Is it proposed to allow this section 27 to stand for further consideration?

Yes.
Section 27 stands.
Sections 28 and 29 agreed to.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish this committee to have any misunderstanding. We have passed clause 25-
There is a section missing.
Which included form No. 36, but I did not hear you call section 26 of this act.
No, it appears to be missing.
I mean section 26 at the bottom of page 26. I have not heard that section called. It may be because I did not understand, but that section 26 is important.
If my hon. friend has any remarks to make let us go back to section 26.
It is not a case of my making any remarks, it is a question of this committee passing 26.
My hon. friend misunderstands me. If my hon. friend did not hear 26 being called let us go back to it, because I would be delighted to hear from him.

It is not a question of
hearing from me. I have nothing to say, but every section should be called.
It was called.
Then I am in error, but I did not hear section 26 called.
Well, it was called.
I was listening carefully. If section 26 was called there is no doubt about it. I have no objection then to going to 27.

May I call the attention
of the committee to section 27 which has been allowed to stand? The chief electoral officer, during the course of his period in office, came to the conclusion that a large number of constituencies which were not now in the schedule of what I might call two-week constituencies, that is to say, between nomination day and election day two weeks must elapse, should be added. For instance, in the western provinces: Manitoba-Brandon, Dauphin, Lisgar, Macdonald, Marquette, Neepawa, Portage la Prairie, Souris; in Saskatchewan-

Dominion Elections Act
Assiniboia Humboldt, Ivindersley, Last Mountain, Long Lake, Mackenzie, Melville, Moose Jaw, Qu'Appelle, Rosetown, Saskatoon, South Battleford, Swift Current, Weyburn, Willow Bunch, Yorkton; in Alberta-Acadia, Battle River, Bow River, Calgary West, Cam-rose, Lethbridge, Medicine Hat, Red Deer, Yegreville, Wetaskiwin. It was suggested in the committee that members of parliament who thought it was in the public interest that their constituencies should be placed in the schedule could have the same done by way of amendment.
But election day would be the same for all of those constituencies.
Yes.
With regard to section 29, would the Solicitor General say whether that applies to past elections or future elections?

Future elections. The committee was of opinion that these amendments should apply only at the next general election, that they should not apply to the by-elections which will be held during the present parliament.
But if the present members of parliament are candidates at the general election will this apply to them or not?
Any member of the present parliament.
What about future parliaments?

The act is amended for that purpose, and we have this last clause saying:
This act shall not apply to the election of any member to the present parliament.

It seems to affect
general elections as well as byelections.
It will be in force at the next general election.

Could not that be stated
a little more clearly?

I do not know how it
could be worded any more clearly than it is; the word "to" makes it perfectly clear. It is not "of."
Section stands.
On section 4-Polling day to be half holiday.

I suggest that instead
of taking the clause which is now in the
bill we should go back to the old clause and substitute the word "three" for the word "two" in the second line thereof. That would give the employee three hours in which to vote and it would not deprive him of pay for any portion of time on election day.

Why does he need three
hours-to have a drink?

In parts of Winnipeg
many persons work as far as ten miles away from their polling division.

I understand that the government have no objection to accepting this amendment, but as chairman of the committee I wish to dissociate myself from it. We considered the matter thoroughly and came to the conclusion that the federal parliament had no authority to grant a holiday with pay.
With compulsory pay.

There is, it is true, a clause
in the Dominion Elections Act providing that every employer shall on polling day allow every elector, his employee, at least two additional hours in which to vote and that no employer shall make any deduction from the [DOT]pay of such employee. I think it is a question of civil rights and contract and not one for the federal parliament.
Section stands.

speechtext: With the consent -of the house I desire to move that the amendments made by the Senate to Bill 84, to incorporate the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada, be now read a first and second time and concurred in.

Motion agreed to, amendments read the first and second times and concurred in.
C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal

The house resumed from May 27 consideration in committee of Bill No. 254, respecting the construction by the Canadian National Railway Company of certain terminal facilities with grade separation and other works at and in the vicinity of t'he city of Montreal.-Mr. Dunning.-Mr. Johnston in the chair.

Certain sections of this
bill were allowed to stand in order to give me an opportunity to consult the law officers in order to make sure that the intentions which I expressed to the house and which were agreeable to the house really had been carried into effect in the bill. A careful check of the matter with the law officers of the department and those of the Department of Justice convinces me that the bill as drafted does in fact leave the Board of Railway Commissioners in exactly the same position with reference to this work as they would be in reference to any other piece of work done by the Canadian National, but in order to establish that fact beyond question and to satisfy the house generally as to the clarity of the legislation, in connection with section 7, which was allowed to stand, I propose to eliminate these words, commencing on line 13:
Detail plans of crossings of railways and crossings by the railway of streets or highways shall be subject to the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners.
By the elimination of those words there can be no doubt but that the provisions of the Railway Act with respect to the powers and duties of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and those of the Canadian National Railway Act, will apply to the works contemplated by this bill.
In connection with section 8 a similar question^ was brought up by the hon. member for South Toronto, and I now propose a redrafted section in order to make it quite clear that the matters dealt with in this section are not within the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners in any case, and to provide a manner whereby they may be dealt with. The redrafted section reads:
Where streets or highways are affected by the said works but are not crossed by the company's tracks or diverted incidental to any suoh crossing and by reason thereof the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada has no jurisdiction under the Railway Act with respect thereto, the company may with the approval of tire governor in council, enter into agreements, where it may be desirable, with the city of Montreal or with any other municipality with respect to such streets or highways or with respect to the opening of new streets, the closing ot existing streets and ways, the making of 
diversions or widenings of such streets or highways, and the making of sub-streets, subways or overhead facilities in connection with such streets or highways, and the apportionment of the cost thereof.
I think that amendment will make it quite clear that the agreement contemplated is one with respect to improvements, which, under the Railway Act, are not within the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners.
Many objections were offered to section 10 of the bill, and I propose to move that that section be struck out. I think these amendments will meet the various objections raised the last time this bill was in committee.

Mr. Chairman, before this
amendment is taken up I would like to take this opportunity to present a few views on this matter. This proposed station will not be a union station, but a station for one railway only. Does the minister propose the same equality of treatment for other places as for Montreal herein?
The port of Montreal has developed in a wonderful manner. The city of Toronto has had to pay about $12,000,000 to have a viaduct constructed there. During the past eight years, since I have been a member of this house, the Dominion of Canada expended $15,000,000 to construct a great bridge at Montreal. This parliament should only be concerned with interprovincial or international bridges, or where navigation is affected, but the Dominion government paid the full cost of this purely municipal bridge for the city of Montreal or a bridge between two provincial municipalities. A great real estate movement is taking place in the city of Montreal in connection with this particular proposition. Land is being bought up by speculators whereas the whole business should be handled by the government. The government could buy more land than is needed and then take advantage of the unearned increment. The city of Montreal should be contributing 50 per cent of the cost of this work. In the old days of the railway commission, the late Mr. Justice Mabee gave a ruling which affected every municipality making an application for the removal of level crossings. His ruling was that where the highway had been there ahead of the railway, the railway paid, but where the railway had been there first then the municipality should shoulder the whole burden of the work.
The city of Toronto gave the Canadian Pacific Railway a right of way down the Don river for $600 per year, when it would have cost them hundreds of thousands of dollars to get into the heart of the city. The

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
city leased the station site, that is the new union station site, to the Grand Trunk for a station and the railway leased part of it to the post office. The cost of the station at Toronto will come to about $6,000,000, while the viaduct will cose about $32,000,000. The member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) said that it would cost $10,000,000 before they got through, but the city of Toronto will have to pay over $12,000,000 in order to provide a viaduct and rights of way for the railways for a distance of fifteen miles along the water front. The minister's amendment does not cover this phase at all; the railway commission cannot change the agreement between the government of Canada and the Canadian National Railways and a third party, such as the city of Montreal. They cannot interfere with vested rights; their duty is to enforce the Railway Act and any provisions of that act as to plans, routes, and other technical layouts.
I have no desire to cripple the national railways, far from it; I hope they grow in strength from year to year. I think they have been doing far better than anyone expected. This burden of $50,000,000 is being put upon the shoulders of the taxpayers of Canada. If this amount -were not being expended in this way reduction in the income tax and sales tax would be possible but the government insists upon continuing to spend money like water. It seems to me that this particular matter might stand over for a while. The government should say to the city of Montreal, "We are not going to continue to place the municipal burdens of the city of Montreal upon the people of Canada." New highways, town planning, new subways, widening of street, and other local improvements are to be made at the cost of the people of Canada. The principle property and civil rights in the province is involved when a municipality receives consideration of this kind. If the minister were up and doing he would say to the people of Montreal, "It is nearly time that the municipality paid for its own municipal work," and not have that cost saddled upon the people of the province of Ontario and other provices in the Dominion of Canada. The rest of the country has been asked to pay too much money for the benefit of this municipality: this city is well able to take care of its own municipal burdens.
If this were a union station the argument might be a little different. The suggestion was made that union station should be built in the city of Hamilton, to be used by the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Toronto, Hamilton & Buffalo Railway, and the Grand
Trunk, but nothing has come of that proposition. The city of Hamilton, like Toronto, was asked to contribute. The government can build an elevator in Port Huron, which might just as well hiave been built in Sarnia, and they are quite content to pay the cost of the elaborate improvements which are being made in the city,of Detroit instead of having that city pay a fair share of the cost of those Canadian National improvements.
This is a very improvident bargain as far as the people of Canada are concerned, and it might very well stand for another year. The government should ask the city of Montreal to pay $20,000,000 towards the cost of this work. The time has come for someone to stand up and say something about this matter. Does the minister propose similar equality of treatment for the other cities in the Dominion, or similar gradte separation? If that is the case, then the city of Toronto would have a good claim for a refund of the money it has paid. In 1911, 1912 and 1913 we attempted to arrive at an agreement with the railway commission, but we were told that not a dollar would be spent in Toronto unless we came across with $10,000,000 or $15,000,000 for the grade separation viaduct work along the waterfront. I do not know of any state government in the United States that is doing this for the municipalities. Certainly the state of New York would not do it. The cities of Buffalo, Rochester and Cleveland have had to spend millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money in order to carry out similar improvements. If you go along lake Erie, the cities of Toledo and Detroit have had to spend money to remedy the evils of these level crossings. If the city of Montreal is to go scot-free in regard to level crossings and bridges as well, what is the next municipal service that that city will want the Dominion to pay for? It will mot be long before they want the country as a whole to pay for a new trunk sewer service or a new water supply. If you read the Municipal Act in the Code of Quebec, you will find that these services are all municipal. I have looked over the situation and what is proposed to be done is nothing but municipal town planning. The government is going to contribute more than half of this money in order to do town planning in Montreal. Look at the own planning in Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton, where they have widened boulevards which are a great credit to the people of those cities. Are they going to come to parliament to ask the government to pay part of their cost out of the public treasury? No. If we are going to pass this legislation, there will be an

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
agitation made to the government for the refund of the cost of improvements such as these. The city of Toronto could make out a strong case for a refund of $10,000,000 for viaduct work from this parliament.
The port of Montreal is one of the largest ports in the world. The administration of that port is not, I think, excelled anywhere else, and the people are going to get back every dollar spent on that port. But as regards this local town planning scheme, a very strong case could' be and has been made out that the city of Montreal should shoulder some of these burdens itself and not unload its town planning and other municipal improvements upon the Dominion.
