speechtext:
Section 10 has been
struck out.

I was about to suggest.
to the minister, looking at the bill in its amended form, that it would make it perfectly clear if a special section were added stating that matters with respect to the crossing of streets or highways by railways and the crossing of railways by streets or highways, shall be subject to the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners as provided by the Railway Act. As the bill stands now, there is no reference as to how the matter is to be dealt with. My hon. friend's submission is that the provisions of the Railway Act will therefore apply. Might it not be desirable to state in the bill itself that the provisions

of the Railway Act with respect to crossings of railways and so forth Shall apply? I am offering this as a suggestion, and another suggestion which I have in mind and which, I suspect from the conversation I have had wdth the minister, he will not accept, is that an amendment be made to the legislation by adding a section declaring that:
This act shall come into force on proclamation by the governor in council after approval of the plans of the said works by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
That is the whole scheme?

Yes. I am still most
desirous, if possible, of bringing about a simplicity of terminals which, admittedly, this does not do. Whether or not, as I already said to the minister the other day, if an opportunity were afforded before an independent tribunal for all parties concerned to be heard, a plan might result that would bring about the creation of union facilities, I cannot say, but I have thought a great deal about this. I sent to the library and got the life of the late J. J. Hill for the purpose of refreshing my memory about what he said of the desirability of great terminals in a large city like Montreal. I have not forgotten the fact that these terminals can in no sense be made profitable by passenger traffic.
I remember that the president of the road has said that the passenger traffic produces no profit so far as this terminal is concerned, and I realize that something between $4,000,000 and $5,000,000 per annum must be provided by the traffic on the system to pay interest and depreciation upon those properties. The amount may be a little more. When I say that, I mean not only the sum now presently contemplated to be spent, but the $12,500,000, authorized and expended on the previous scheme, together with the accumulated interest which is large, and the $1,500,000 of securities which the hon. member mentioned the other day. This means that when the property is completed five or six years hence, it will involve a fixed annual charge of between $4,000,000 and $5,000,000, and if my idea as to the ultimate cost is fairly correct, the fixed annual charge will be nearer $5,000,000 than $4,000,000. That money will not in any sense be made out of passenger traffic except that there may be in suburban areas some passenger traffic th&t may be profitable. Within the last five years the Illinois Central have spent $30,000,000 in terminal facilities in Chicago. They have changed from steam to electricity, and the result has been that a loss of $5,000,000 in the terminal traffic

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
of the Illinois Central has been converted into a yearly profit of SI,000,000, a change altogether of $6,000,000 by reason of an expenditure of $30,000,000 in electrifying the terminal facilities and suburban lines of the Illinois Central in and about the city of Chicago. That is an exceptional situation owing to the lake front and the heavy congestion of passenger traffic to the east of the city of Chicago, providing revenue on a very large scale.
This scheme has been described in some quarters as ambitious. It must be so, if the principles in connection with terminals as laid down by Mr. Hill are to prevail. After all. a great railway must have great terminals. It must look to the future. It is not sufficient to look to to-day. It must look beyond the conditions of to-day and see tomorrow, and more than to-morrow; it must see the day after.
There are acute differences between the two systems with reference to these terminals. The minister and I have discussed this matter. One system thinks that a through traffic terminal is not necessary. The other says that a through traffic terminal is essential both for traffic south, east and west. I realize that the expenditure of money sometimes is the best method' to ensure the making of money. In other words, I realize that money that is not profitable can at times be made profitable by the expenditure of large sums of money.
I have not forgotten the boldness of Mr. Harriman and the courage with which he crossed Salt lake at an expenditure of $9,000,000. with a short cut-off or his construction of 332 miles of road to take the place of 374 miles of abandoned road, in order to make large sums of money. I am not unmindful of other similar instances in the history of railroading, but I am also remembering that this is a country of only 10,000,000 people.
There is one factor that I hope the minister will not overlook. We own a railroad a very considerable portion of which is in the United States, and the .president of the road1 has told U3 that the most profitable mileage that we have to-day is that portion of the Grand Trunk that lies in the United States. That is a very serious situation because it must be admitted by every thoughtful observer that when you have a very substantial section of your national railway in another country, the question as to its profitable operation does not depend on anything that you can do, but depends upon conditions as to traffic that exist in that other country, together with the maintenance of a rate that will enable a profit
to be made. We have no control over those conditions. We cannot control the situation on the Vermont section as to profit and loss after we have completed our investment and taken up our receivers' certificates. We cannot change the situation in respect to Portland and the terminals there, or in respect to the Grand Trunk Western and all that is involved in the consolidation of the many lines included in the system. These are matters that are beyond our control, and at the present time some sections of the road are highly profitable. We realize in the light of what the president of our own railway has said that we must rely on freight traffic proper to pay the annual interest and charges on this terminal; in other words, passenger traffic will produce no profit, and that directly affects every producer of freight on the system. It affects the man on the prairie, the manufacturer in the east, the automobile manufacturer to some extent on the Grand Trunk Western lines, and I d'o not think it would be too much to ask that before these plans are finally acted upon by the governor in council the whole matter should be considered by an independent tribunal. I confess to the .minister that in looking about for that independent tribunal, the only reason why I fixed upon the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada was because it is the only tribunal which is charged under our general laws with responsibility in connection with railroads. I do not say that I think it is the best tribunal in the world. There are many difficulties that I see. Mr. Ruel's view is that it is undesirable to submit any Canadian National railway matters to the Board of Railway Commissioners. In putting this amendment before the minister for his consideration I apprehend, as he said to me in discussing the matter, that he may not accept it, and that it may be my duty when the bill is read a third time to-morrow-formally to offer this amendment for the consideration of the house.
I had not intended to speak at such length at the moment, but I do confess after having followed the development of the railroad situation in Canada with a good deal of interest for the last thirty years, and having been particularly interested in it in the days of the old Grand Trunk and National Transcontinental, I ventured upon the role of a prophet and made a prediction which, though it was not generally accepted at the time I made it, proved to be right in the end, and both Alberta and Saskatchewan were called upon to pay on their guarantees of interest on branch lines of $13,000 and $15,000 a mile respectively.
303G

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
Few people realize what it has meant to those provinces to have the national railways consolidated. Had they not -been consolidated and taken over by the crown, a burden would have been imposed upon the provinces that would have been very considerable and although some people think that British Columbia would 'have escaped, I think that thoughtful observers who have studied the economics of the situation, as did at least one of the directors of the Canadian National, who is now the deputy minister, will agree' that the province of British Columbia would have been called upon to pay substantial sums of money but for the taking over of the Canadian Northern iby the crown. Bearing in mind the six or seven lean years that Joseph experienced in Egypt, which lean years have also been known in Canada, and that these days will come again, and that somebody must find between $4,500,000 and $5,000,000 every year to pay the interest on the investment which we will have in these terminal facilities, I have made the suggestion I have. I am sorry the minister feels that it cannot 'be accepted. I shall have to turn over in my own mind the desirability of submitting the suggestion in the form of a formal amendment when the bill is under consideration for third reading.
I want to say that the minister has approached this matter certainly not with a desire to press it upon the house in a sense of it being a government measure, although, of course, it is a government measure, and he has endeavoured to eliminate, by striking out the section to which I directed attention the other day, and in making the changes which he has submitted to the house to-day, those sources of difficulty which I think he will admit the experience of the past has taught us are present, with a view to ensuring so far as possible that there shall be a minimum of such difficulties to be encountered in connection with this undertaking; but there are still many matters of great moment that will rest for their solution upon the discretion and ability and fidelity of the men concerned. It is for these reasons that I have ventured to make this suggestion to the minister, and as the bill will not be read a third time to-day I shall in the meantime consider whether or not it will be desirable to submit a formal amendment.

I shall not deal with the remarks of the hon. member for Toronto Northwest for the reason that it is quite apparent that he is under a complete misapprehension as to the scope and purpose of the bill before the houoe, and the leader of [Mr. Bennett. J
the opposition and others I feel sure would not associate themselves with his remarks in that connection.
With regard to the suggestion of the leader of the opposition, as I stated at the outset careful consideration was given to the suggestion which he made, and I fully appreciate the force of his remarks just now in relation to the importance to the national system of that portion of the railway which is located in the United States. I should not like, and I feel sure that he would not like, his remarks to be interpreted as implying that the national system is dependent for its profitable operation upon that part which is located within the United States. Some 1,600 miles out of a total of 22,000 miles in the system are located in the United States.

I did not say that the
system was dependent upon it.
I was saying that I felt sure my hon. friend would not want that impression left.
I made it perfectly clear that the president had said that that was Ihe most profitable mileage which they had. That is on record.

I am not disputing the record; I was proceeding to analyse it in order that there might not 'be an impression left *n the country by the hon. gentleman's remarks that the system was in any sense dependent upon its American mileage. Some 900 odd miles of that American mileage, which is comprised in what we call the Grand Trunk Western system, undoubtedly is the most profitable 900 miles of the system, but it is only 900 miles out of a total of 22,000 miles. The rest of our American mileage, comprised within the Vermont Central, of something over 400 miles, and the line down to Portland in the neighbourhood of 200 miles, cannot be described as exceptional money-makers, but I would not depreciate for a moment the value of the Grand Trunk Western portion of the system.
I wish to examine for a moment my hon. friend's suggestion that he might move an amendment on the third reading. I do so in order that we may get an appreciation of what it would mean, and in order that the house may get an appreciation of the reasons which prompt the government in hesitating very much to accept any such suggestion. In connection with the expenditure of any money on railroads in Canada, whether publicly or privately owned, the first move

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
would be the action of the proprietor in authorizing their management to expend the money, and we are, as I pointed out the other day in this house, in the position of representing the proprietors.
That is the government.
Parliament.
No, it is the governor in council.

Parliament is conferring
authority upon the governor in council to authorize the management to expend, under terms set out by parliament, the moneys dealt with in this bill. The proprietorial relationship must not be lost sight of. The Board of Railway Commissioners has, under the law with respect to all railways, a very definite function, and it is not in any sense to be confused with the function of proprietorship; they are not in the position under the law of advising the proprietors of a railway as to how and upon what works the proprietors should expend their own money.
Not their own money.
The proprietor's money.

Not the railways' own
money.

The proprietor's money I said. The Board of Railway Commissioners, to put it in a manner I feel sure my hon. friend will not disagree with, is not under the statute creating it placed in a position where it can advise the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian National Railways, or any other railway, as to the manner in which those railways shall expend the money of the proprietors. The function of the Board of Railway Commissioners is judicial as between those proprietors represented by their management and the public who may be affected by the works which are to be built, constructed or operated with the moneys which the proprietors have allocated for that purpose. My hon. friend, I am sure, sees the principle I am trying to point out. In no other case has it ever been proposed that the Board of Railway Commissioners should be called in to pass upon what the proprietors themselves should authorize to be expended upon their own works. But the Board of Railway Commissioners are always authorized to come in and examine the relationship between that expenditure and the rights of the public, or the rights of individuals in relation thereto. We are proposing in this case to preserve intact the functions of the Board of Railway Commissioners and their relationship to undertakings of this character. And I hesitate very much to establish that, in addition to exercising that function, which is judicial in character, the Board1 of Railway Commissioners should assume one of the functions of management in determining the nature of the works to be built with the moneys provided by the proprietor. That is the matter of principle wthich I had in mind as an objection to what is proposed by my hon. friend.
Having said that, let me go further and say. that so far as the government is concerned it is under no illusions as to the far-reaching character of proposals of this kind. The government appreciates to the full the responsibility of embarking upon an enterprise of this kind. But we all recognize, all of parliament I think recognizes, representing as we wo the proprietors, that this is something which we must undertake. We have, whether we will or not the responsibility, and the final responsibility for the operation of two billion dollars' worth of the people's property in this railway system. And here is a problem which has been studied for many years, a problem which is recognized on all hands as one which is crying for solution as no other single problem on the railroad is crying for solution. A result of the studies which have been made by the officials of the railway and 'by the management, has been submitted to outside opinion; that outside opinion has been submitted to the house, and we have gone as far as we think we can go in that direction. But, nevertheless, I would say to my hon. friend this; the government does not take the position that the door is closed in so far as unionizing this work is concerned. I think I can say that with the entire concurrence of the government.

What do you mean by
" unionizing "7 It seems to me an awful word.

Making of the terminal
a union terminal. The door in that respect is not closed. The door in that respect will not be closed during the years in which the project is being developed, during the building years; it will still be open for other parties desiring to come in and to create of this project a union terminal; the door will still be open for them to do so; the field for negotiation is still open.

That means the field with
regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway?
C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal

Absolutely. It is still
open. But we may as well face the facts, Mr. Chairman. The leader of the opposition stated them in one way. I will state the same set of facts in another way although there would not be any difference of opinion between us as to what the facts are. They were related in the committee and again when this matter wAs before the house previously, that the Canadian Pacific Railway does not believe that a union terminal at the tunnel site would be suitable or economical from the point of view of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian .National Railways do not believe that a union station at Windsor street would be suitable or economical from the point of view of the best interests of the Canadian National Railways. That difference does exist. We cannot overcome it. The leader of the opposition the other day pointed out very clearly that the only way to overcome it would be to exercise the powers of this parliament to force one or the other to go into the terminal of the other. And no one has yet suggested that the power of parliament should be used to force the Canadian Pocific Railway to go into the tunnel terminal, and no one has yet suggested that the power of parliament should be exercised upon the Canadian National Railways to force them to go into Windsor street. The issues are too great for parliament to attempt to exercise force in connection with that matter.
That is, I think, all I have to say on the matter. I trust my hon. friend will appreciate the reasons which prompt me in hesitating very much to set up the Board of Railway Commissioners as advisers to the management of any railway. To my mind it would impair, and possibly conflict with, the operation of their judicial function which they would undoubtedly be called upon to exercise in connection with many phases of the same matter.

Of course, the minister
appreciates that the commission could be authorized to do so. I felt after looking casually through the report that the hon. minister was good enough to give me the other day that if the wealth of learning about terminals that could be brought before the commission was brought before the commission by experts of outstanding ability on this continent it might create such a situation as would inevitably induce the management, of the two enterprises to go into a union station enterprise. I might say that I wholly agree with my hon. friend that the commission as such is neither qualified nor empowered to 
compel either one road or the other to take the action suggested, but my hope had been rather that with the evidence that might be brought before the commission as such the deferring of the coming into force of the act would bring about such a state of affairs as might induce the parties affected to realize the desirability of taking the action which we so much desire, and thereby lessen what I conceive to be a very heavy load to be borne by our national system. That is the whole reason behind my suggestion. I did not go into detail because I thought the minister realized that I was not for a moment suggesting that some of his appointees on the Board of Railway Commissioners would be the best people to determine on a plan of the magnitude of the one now before the house.

I had in mind previously that my hon. friend apparently had more faith at this stage in the Board of Railway Commissioners than he had at an earlier stage in the session. But I would say in that regard, to repeat in rather more amplified fashion what I said a moment ago, so far as ithe government is concerned, in authorizing the carrying on of these works, the door is still ' open. And, of course, as my hon. friend knows, it is within the power of the government, if the government so determines, to refer any matter such as this to the Board of Railway Commissioners. And I can go as far as this: If there does appear any hope of a solution, more advantageous to the country, to the national system and to the Canadian Pacific system, being arrived at by conference or in any other way, the government will not hesitate to use the power which it has to refer to the Board of Railway Commissioners any question the solution of which might involve a better scheme or a better arrangement than the one now proposed.

Has not the railway commission power to compel the railway companies to have a union station in any town?
Is that out of their jurisdiction entirely?
They have no such power.

I find very confusing indeed the explanation of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) with regard to proprietorship and the suggestion that the members of this house represent the proprietors. Is it not clearly expressed in this bill, and in the other enactments which apply to the Canadian National Railways, as an entity in itself, that it so far comes under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners [DOT] that, acting in its judicial capacity,

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
the board has the same jurisdiction to decide as between the Canadian National Railways and any other public interest, as between the Canadian National Railways and any city or municipality, and as between the Canadian National Railways and the harbour commission of Montreal, for example, in so far as the Canadian National is a railway corporation, as it has when any similar issue arises between the Canadian Pacific Railway and any public interest, between the Canadian Pacific Railway and any municipality, or between the Canadian Pacific Railway and any other public corporation?

The only difference is- I think this has been mentioned before-that with respect to the approval of actual detailed plans of a railroad, the Canadian National Railways, by virtue of its original statute enacted in 1919, is required to secure the approval of the Minister of Railways, whereas any other railway is required to secure the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Subject to that one qualification, what my hon. friend says is perfectly correct as to the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners over the Canadian National Railway. But I cannot understand what the hon. member means about being confused as to the term proprietor which I used. The proprietors of an ordinary railway are, of course, the shareholders.

We all know that, of
course; it passes without comment. But we are not dealing with this matter now as merely the proprietors of the Canadian National Railways; we are dealing with it as the parliament of Canada, giving powers to an institution known as the Canadian National Railways which we have already constituted by statutes of this parliament. I would rather deal with the matter from that point of view, and I do still think that in all respects in which the Board of Railway Commissioners, as a judicial body, has jurisdiction as between, for instance, the Canadian Pacific Railway and any public interest, or between the Canadian Pacific Railway and any municipal or civic interest, or between the Canadian Pacific Railway and any other corporation constituted by this parliament, the Board of Railway Commissioners might well have the same jurisdiction when a similar issue arises between the Canadian National Railways and such bodies as I have mentioned.

The section in the Railway Act to which the minister has referred is not broad enough to enable him to make 78594-193
reference to the board. I looked it up the other day and this was one of the reasons that impelled me to offer the suggestion I did. The section in question is 69:
(1)	The board may appoint or direct any person to make an inquiry and report upon any application, complaint or dispute pending before the board, or upon any matter or thing over which the board has jurisdiction under this or the special act.
(2)	The minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, appoint and direct any person to inquire into and report upon any matter or thing which the minister is authorized to deal with under this act or the special act.
The limitation as to the reference is that it must be a matter which the minister is authorized to deal with under the Railway Act or under the special act.

Under this act.
M. BENNETT: But this is a special act empowering the minister to deal with a limited number of matters. For instance, the very section with which we were dealing, section 7, authorizes the Minister of Railways to deal with the question of railways and canals and the crossing of canals. The Minister of Marine must deal with the harbour of Montreal, but the minister is not as such authorized to deal with the plan as a whole.
I will give my hon. friend the section in a moment.
I do not think my hon. friend's construction can be placed upon it.
Take the beginning of section 7; that will help my hon. friend.

Very well. That section begins:
The general plan or plans of the said works and amendments or additions to such general plan at any time made, shall, on the recommendation of the Minister of Railways and Canals, be subject to the approval of the governor in council.
But that is mot the point. What we are dealing with is, for instance, the question of cost. We have had no details yet as to the question of cost; no engineers' estimates have been submitted. We have merely men standing up and saying that in their opinion it will cost so much. But this vote is for $50,000,000. So far as we are aware, it might be $10,000,000, because that is all that is to foe spent this year; and the total cost as said to be $51,400,000. It is abundantly dear that four years from now, if the appropriations overrun, the matter is to be dealt with in the way I have indicated; and the only difficulty I see is this-and the minister put his finger on it a moment ago: How is the governor iD



C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
council to obtain its knowledge to deal with this matter in t'he public interest, representing the people of Canada as a whole, as distinguished from its political action as the government of the day? It was for that reason that I made the suggestion I did, rather than that the matter should be dealt with simply by the governor in council. In other words, I was endeavouring to ensure that there should be detailed information in connection with this matter placed before some tribunal that would approve generally of the enterprise, beyond mere statements such as I heard the other day-I do not care how long the situation has been studied-and the views of the minister himself. The minister knows more about, this matter than any other member of the government; yet I venture to say that if I examined him to-day I could within a few minutes indicate that his knowledge was not such as would warrant him in undertaking to expend such large sums of money if he were in the position he once occupied in connection with a great industry in western Canada. In short, he has not secured that detailed information which he would insist upon having in connection with any enterprise he had to do with, before authorizing so relatively large an expenditure as that which is here involved. All I am urging is that the approval should be secured of some body, with a volume of expert testimony behind it, as to the cost of the scheme, the plans, feasibility, general relation to the future, the adequacy of all the facilities, and every other question involved in the undertaking, having regard to what Mr. Hill pointed out as being in the ultimate analysis the important thing to consider. I was trying to make sure that all these matters would be dealt with before the minister and the government were pushed- I am not using the word offensively-into the position where they had to decide upon some course of action.

I should like to illustrate
what I had in mind a moment ago when I addressed a question to the minister. The last three lines of section 7 are as follows:
Detail plans affecting the property of the harbour commissioners of Montreal shall be subject to the approval of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
The harbour commission of Montreal is a corporate body having certain express powers delegated to it by this parliament; the members of that board have a practical knowledge of the conditions of their property and a large experience in dealing with the whole undertaking. Suppose a difference of opinion arises

between the management of the Canadian National Railways and the harbour commission, with respect to detail plans which affect the property of the harbour commissioners of Montreal. Should not such a difference of opinion be referred for settlement to a judicial body such as the Board of Railway Commissioners?

This has reference to
detail plans.

Yes, and those are the important plans. If this section provided that general plans should be first approved by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that would have had another signification, but the actual plans which are prepared by the management of the Canadian National Railways, when once approved by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, will have full force and effect in so far as they affect the property of the Montreal harbour commission. I do not think the political head of such a department as that of Marine and Fisheries should have the sole and exclusive decision in regard to issues which may arise, which are likely to arise and which in my opinion inevitably will arise between the harbour commissioners of Montreal and the executive of the Canadian National Railways in carrying out the detail plans for this enormous development. I am not in the confidence of the harbour commissioners at all; I have not approached them nor have they approached me, but I am sure they have very definite opinions as to the best method of carrying to completion those terminal facilities having regard to that harbour, and I understand that the leader of the opposition has suggested that in matters of this kind, where issues arise between the Canadian National Railways and other corporate public bodies, those issues might well be placed before a judicial body such as the Board of Railway Commissioners.

The point raised by
my hon. friend is of some importance, but I should like to explain why the particular phrase to which he is referring was inserted in this bill. It will be noticed that in the first part of section 7 the authority to approve of general plans is given the governor in council, upon the recommendation of the Minister of Railways and Canals. In connection with the detail plans affecting an enterprise which, in its relation to parliament, is under the overseeing eye, if I may use that term, of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, it was thought that in case any difficulty arose between the harbour board and the railway

C.N.R-Montreal Terminal
executive the hatbour board should not be placed in the position of having to appeal to the Minister of Railways, but rather to that minister who is particularly charged with looking after harbours and harbour interests.

Does not that mean that
the issue will be settled by political considerations?
I cannot quite see that.

Let us assume for the
moment that grave differences of opinion do arise between the harbour board and the management of the railways, just such issues as might arise between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the harbour board, with reference to electrification or any other matters which might come up. It would take us days to consider these plans in all their details. Now, why should that decision be left to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; what special knowledge does he possess of matters of this kind? I am not speaking particularly of the present minister, but what equipment, what qualifications are possessed by the minister presiding over the Department of Marine and Fisheries which enable him to decide intricate engineering problems such as those which may arise between these two corporate bodies? Why should such issues be left to the decision of a mere political head; why should they not be left to the Board of Railway Commissioners, who at least have expert advisers to assist them and who have a procedure, a practice and a method whereby they may summon all interests affected and hear expert evidence as the basis for their decision?

I might point out to my hon. friend that this does not take away any of the powers otherwise possessed by the Board of Railway Commissioners; if the matters affecting the property of the Montreal Harbour Board do come within the purview of the Board of Railway Commissioners, under the Railway Act, then their approval certainly must be secured. As a matter of fact my hon. friend is inaccurate in one particular; he says that the plans do involve works on the property of the Montreal Harbour Board. That is not the case.

I may be mistaken, of course, but on the plan I saw that line running through property which either has been acquired or is in process of being acquired by the board of harbour commissioners, and I think issues are likely to arise in that connection. Perhaps I should not say so decidedly that these issues are likely to arise, but they may arise, and it is so probable that they will arise that in the bill before us the min-78594-193J
ister is providing a method of determining such issues if they come to a head. By the express terms of this section he has placed the power to make such a decision entirely within the discretion of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries who, while he has a certain oversight over the Montreal haifeour commissioners, should not it seems to me be vested with jurisdiction to decide issues which may arise as between those harbour commissioners and the management of the Canadian National Railways. I do not think I can say more.

Just to complete what
I was saying regarding the harbour commission property and the work to be done thereon, I might say that the plans contemplated by this bill cover work to be done by the Canadian National Railways which will connect the harbour commission's tracks. The plans contemplate also certain work which will be carried out by the harbour commission and which it is agreeable to carry out. I would point out to my hon. friend that the Montreal harbour commission have been made fully aware of the contents of this bill as they relate to themselves, and that commission is quite satisfied with the arrangements made.

My information was that
they had not 'been fully consulted. I was not told that by one of the harbour commissioners, but received my information from another source. Why vest in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries the sole discretion of deciding such issues as they arise?

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter which should be included' in this particular bill, and that is provision for the electrification of the system within the city of Montreal. The railway is to be elevated over certain portions of the city but, as far as I can see, there is nothing in the bill which provides that the system shall be electrified. Electrification is absolutely necessary; otherwise the undertaking will be most destructive to property in the vicinity. We are suffering a great deal of inconvenience at the present time due to the non-electrification of the railways within the limits of the oitjr; in fact, I believe Montreal is the only city on the American continent which puts up with the smoke nuisance existing in the city. We are suffering from the operations of the Canadian Pacific Railway as well as from those of the Canadian National Railways, and I think something should be done to ensure that in densely populated municipalities the health of the people shall not be endangered by the continued use of coal-burning locomotives
C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal

within the municipal limits. I had hoped that provision would have 'been made in this bill for the electrification of the system within the city limits. I believe that all railway systems within the city of Montreal should be electrified.

Mr. Chairman, with
regard to the suggestion of the hon. member for St. Ann (Mr. Guerin), I might inform the committee that it is proposed to electrify the tunnel.

The tunnel is electrified
now.

To provide for tihe increased traffic which will be brought about by the completion of this larger scheme. The Canadian National Railway has conducted some very successful experiments and tests in the use of Diesel locomotives, and it is proposed to use Diesel powered locomotives very extensively in the operation of the terminal scheme.
The matter of general electrification comes within the realm of railway economics. Such schemes depend upon the density and the constancy of t'he load, because hon. members will appreciate that the power must be there at all times. The cost of producing the power must be paid whether or not it is uitlized to the fullest extent. I cannot give offhand what might be called the datum point of economical electrical transportation, but there is a point at which the traffic becomes heavy and constant enough to make it economical to electrify a line. For instance, at the present time it would not be good practice to electrify the line between Ottawa and Montreal; the load is not sufficiently constant to make that proposition economically sound, as it would cost far more than to operate under the present method. On the other hand, in a terminal such as the Pennsylvania station in New York city, where the density is ever present, electrical operation is very economical. I can say to my hon. friend from St. Ann that the Canadian National is watching veipr closely the development of traffic densities in and around the city of Montreal, and I can assure him that no time will be lost in putting in such improvements when they are warranted.

Would the use of the
Diesel engines mean that coal would have to be burned?
They are powered by oil.
There would be no smoke?

There is very little.
[Mr. Guerin.l

It is an explosion of oil
rather than the burning of it.

Mr. Chairman, I
would like to take this opportunity of congratulating the citizens of Montreal upon having such excellent terminal facilities for that metropolis of the Dominion of Canada.
What about Quebec?

This city is in the
province of Quebec. They should take great pride in the facilities which are being provided by the Canadian National system. I think the declaration has been made to the house by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals that it is the policy of the Canadian National system to provide proper terminal facilities in most of the large cities of Canada. While I congratulate the citizens of Montreal upon the treatment they are receiving at the hands of the government, I would like to see the people of the old city of Quebec treated in the same manner. Montreal, Toronto and many other cities in this Dominion have been treated quite generously by the Canadian National system while we have been endeavouring for over twenty years to obtain the proper terminal facilities in the city of Quebec. We were told by the government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier that the city of Quebec was the real terminal of the Transcontinental and the Canadian National railway systems, and that we would have proper facilities. We were promised those facilities in 1910, when the Hon. S. N. Parent was chairman of the National Transcontinental railway commission. Proper engineering plans were prepared; a site was decided upon, and a contract was entered into between the city of Quebec and the Transcontinental railway. The city of Quebec consented to give a most valuable property fronting on the St. Lawrence, the Champlain market, a property worth more than $5,000,000. A contract was given to a contracting firm to erect a million-dollar railway station, and there was constructed from the Quebec bridge to that station a road six and a half miles long. After the change of government in 1911, a year later, the contract was cancelled; all work was postponed, and an agreement was entered into between the Transcontinental and the Canadian Pacific whereby the Transcontinental was to use the Canadian Pacific railway facilities at a rate, if I am not mistaken, of $200,000 a year which the Transcontinental paid to bring people into the city of Quebec and then hand them over to their competitor, the Canadian Pacific.

Supply-Pensions and National Health
As I have said, the citizens of Quebec have been making requests of the governments that have been in power from 1911 to 1921, but they have always been told that their requests were under consideration. I remember in 1917 and 191S asking some questions of the then Minister of Railways, the Hon. Doctor Reid, and the then Minister of Public Works, the Hon. Mr. Carvell, and that was the answer which was given. The Minister of Public Works at that time said that the way in which the work had been carried out in the city of Quebec was a tragedy. They admitted that our need was most urgent and1 that something should be done. The present government seems to be well disposed towards the city of Quebec, but we fail to see that anything is being done in our city. A few weeks ago I put a question on the orders of the day, but the same answer was given me by the government, namely, that the matter was under consideration.
Quebec is the oldest and one of the most important cities of the Dominion; it is the only one vdiieh has contributed towards railway development, towards the building of the Quebec and Lake St. John railway and the building of the Canadian Northern railway, and it has given to the Canadian National railway system a property worth more than
85,000,000 in order to obtain proper facilities in the city of Quebec. We are ashamed to say that we are treated as a flag station rather than in the way we should be treated. I do not blame the government, but I say that there is lack of attention on the part of the administration of the system. Sir Henry Thornton does not treat the people of the city and district of Quebec in the way in which we should be treated, and whenever an opportunity is afforded me I will protest as I have done to-day against the way in which we are treated in our city. I am glad to see that the government is dealing so generously with the city of Montreal and I hope it will press the urgency of our needs upon the administration of the railway and do something to render justice to the citizens of Quebec in whose behalf I will continue to protest.

Before we take up any item I would call the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the fact that the air in the chamber is very hot. It is veTy close in here, and I wonder if there is no way in which it can be remedied to give us a chance in this hot weather. Is at not possible to have some of these windows open or electric fans going?

I quite agree with my hon. friend that it is very warm, and just half an hour ago I requested the engineers to see if it was not possible to get in some colder air. The difficulty is that it is pretty hard to find any cold air to-day.
Are these windows permanently fastened?
No, but if they are opened they let in air of a temperature of ninety degrees.

Why not damp the curtains as was done last year and then open the windows? You would then have cooler air in the chamber?

Supply-Public Works-Bridges
Sir GEORGE PEtRLEY: It is not a question of getting cold or hot air, but a question of getting some air.

Just a feiw moments ago I felt just as my hon. friend does and I looked at the thermometers. The one at the end of the chamber read 75 degrees, and the one that I keep here Aows a higher temperature than that. I will read a memorandum that I have just received from my secretary, and I shall be glad to have any suggestions that hon. gentlemen can give:
I have just been down to the basement with the engineer of the building and gone over the machines with him. The air which is being pumped in for ventilation purposes registers ninety degrees. With the machines going as hard as they can, this is being reduced to seventy-six degrees. It has been pointed out, however, that with the windows and doors around the chamber open, hot air is flowing in which is raising the temperature above the temperature of the air which is being pumped into the chamber through the ventilating machines.
I have urged the engineer to keep the machines going just as hard as he can, and to do everything possible to lower the temperature in the chamber.

I have listened to this story from the Minister of Public Works- I am not reflecting on him pereonaly at all'- every time that we have sat here in June. Personally I am tired of these engineers' opinions; I do not think they are any good. Here we are in a stone building and it should be one of the coolest .places in the capital. Even the rooms upstairs are cooler than this chamber. I think it is time that we ignored the opinions of the engineers and got some of these windows open and let this air out. It is a case of letting a breeze through the chamber. The engineers have made a complete fizzle of it, and it is time we tried another scheme. The air is absolutely unbearable here to-day.

The air is being changed
all the time. It is not a question of pumping in fresh air and getting the old air out, because the air is being continually changed. There is no place very cool in the city today.

I differ. You can go into all kinds of residences in the city to-day and be perfectly comfortable, yet this big stone building is one of the most uncomfortable buildings in the city of Ottawa. I think that the ventilation system is defective; I have thought so ever since we came into this new building. I will admit that during the winter this year it was better than past years. I am not criticizing the minister at 
all, but I do not believe that the engineers are familiar with what they should do. This chamber should be a cool chamber, and it is anything but a cool chamber. It is terribly hot.

At times I have seen
it pretty hot in the winter.

The air should be put into circulation by means of fans or something of that kind. The value of that is quite generally recognized. Even if a person is confined to a room, if the air is put in motion he does not suffer. If there is nothing better to be done I tbink it would be well to install a certain number of electric fans to keep the air in circulation and give us a chance to breathe.
I would suggest to the minister that first of all the heat in the radiators should be turned off, because there is heat in these radiators at the present time.

That is right. I found
.heat in the radiators the other day. Somebody did not have the coal supply all burned up.
Damp the curtains and open the windows, and then you oan get fresh air in. We did that last year.

The minister was good enough to allow discussion on any subject relating to public works on this item which stood over. I am desirous of calling his attention again to the fact that there is a very pressing need at the present time of a reasonably small grant for dredging in the harbour of Parry Sound. The harbour of Parry Sound is probably one of the best harbours, if not the best, on the great lakes. It usually has water enough to float any boat on the great lakes, but unfortunately conditions there are somewhat peculiar. The government wharf at that point is situated near the mouth of the Seguin river and below a point where there existed for many years one of the largest sawmills on the Georgian bay. The result of the year's activities of that mill was that a great accumulation of bark and other mill refuse was deposited in the stream. During the last two or three years in succession we have had, unfortunately, high water in the river, and on two or three occasions large dams have broken away causing an extremely heavy flood which moved this mill refuse and deposited it at or about the government wharf. The government have attempted to remedy this condition during the last two years by using one of the

Supply-Public Works-Bridges
boats belonging to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, tying her up to the wharf and endeavouring to blow this sawdust and refuse out of the way by the revolutions of her screw. This has not been successful. The only result has been to blow it away for a distance of about twenty feet immediately opposite the wharf and the refuse has piled up in a heap where it is an obstruction to any boat trying to approach the wharf. The result is that many boats have had difficulty approaching the wharf and some have been unable to tie up to it at all. A large shipping company in Chicago which operates several of the largest passenger -boats on the great lakes runs a seven-day excursion every week from Chicago to various points on the great lakes. The only Canadian -port of call is Parry Sound. These boats carry an average of 800 passengers on each trip, so that they are one of the greatest advertising agencies that we have for Canada. These boats coming in and going out of Parry Sound pass through a part of the Thirty Thousand Islands of the Georgian bay in daylight, both ways. Many people from Chicago take advantage of these weekly trips and become regular tourists in Canada. Many of them have purchased cottages in various parts of northern Ontario. It is very desirable therefore, that these boats continue this service. This steamship company has advised the town council of Parry Sound -that it will be unable to -make Parry Sound during the present season on account of the depth of water, as they have no desire to jeopardize their boats. The matter was taken up with the Department of Public Works, and assurance was given to the council -that a grant would be made sufficient to do this small amount of dredging in order to remove this refuse in front of the wharf during the present season. Well, the main estimates are down and nothing has been put in. After all, these boats are so large that they are tihe ones principally affected. These people visiting Parry Sound on these weekly trips-probably a thousand or fifteen hundred per week-have the privilege of taking back with them to the United States goods to the amount of $100 free of duty, and very many of them take advantage of that privilege. The result is that a large trade has grown up there, principally in woollens and linens, all of which is advantageous to us as Canadians. I would therefore impress upon the minister the necessity of making at least a reasonable grant in the supplementary estimates for this very necessary work. I would also point out that this is not going to be a recurring vote. The
circumstances are as I have stated them. The refuse from this old mill has been swept down and is now lying in front of the government wharf in Parry Sound. When it has been removed there will be no second visitation; everything has been swept a/way and the river is absolutely clear owing to the very heavy freshets that we have had in the last two or three years. I hope the minister will take this into his most serious consideration.

I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend but I will say to him that a deputation interviewed me in regard to this very matter not very long ago-I would say within the last two weeks, probably-and urged upon the department the very things that he has now urged.
I may also say, Mr. Chairman, that this -matter has been before the minister for the last tiwo years.

Well, the information that was given to me by this committee is not as accurate as -I had thought, because I was told that on account of the extra flooding this spring the amount of sawdust and other refuse brought down from -where they formerly had saw mills made the harbour much more impossible of access this spring than it had ever been before. Of course, as my hon. friend knows, the water has been particularly high this year, and this is a matter which comes or could come properly within the category of the things that could not very well have been foreseen at the time the main -estimates weTe prepared. I would say to my hon. friend, however, that it has already received the best consideration the department can give it.

Mr. Chairman, in these dying hours of the session I hesitate to take up very much of the time of the house, especially in view of the extreme heat which many of the thin men in the house feel so greatly. But I have not unduly trespassed on the time of this house during the present session, consequently I feel that it is my duty, on behalf of my constituents in the town of Goderich, to place upon record the great national importance of Goderich harbour, and to try to show t-hat it is a national necessity that the work there should be proceeded with in a more energetic manner.
I have not risen to criticize the Minister of Public Works with regard to the amount placed in the estimates this year for harbour improvements at Goderich, namely $205,000, which, when he viewed Canada from coast to coast, was perhaps the amount he thought

Supply-Public Works-Bridges
we were justly entitled to. I am not at the moment complaining of the amount of the vote. What I am asked (by his own political friends to do is to stress the fact that the work should be proceeded with energetically and that the amount placed in the estimates be spent. (Last year there was placed in the main estimates $75,000 for this purpose, and the people of Goderich and western Ontario were delighted when the minister brought down in the supplementary estimates an additional $100,000. But they were not so delighted when they found at the end of the year that out of this $100,000 which he brought down in the supplementary estimates he had spent only $10,000. The minister may meet with difficulties which I do mot understand, but what we would like to have done is-

Just a moment, so that there may be no misunderstanding. Is my hon. friend under the impression that only $10,000 was spent on the harbour of Goderich last year?
Mr. SPO'TTON: No, I did not say that. I said that $75,000 was brought down in the main estimates. Then the people of the town of Goderich and western Ontario rejoiced to know that the minister had brought down an additional $100,000 in the supplementary estimates. But of this additional $100,000 they were chagrined to learn that only $10,000 was spent. In other words, of the $75,000 in the main estimates and the $100,000 in the supplementary estimates-$175,000 in all-the department expended only $85,000; $90,000 was returned to the treasury and is handed back to us again this year.
This is the point .that I am trying to stress: we are satisfied with the $205,000 which the minister has placed in the estimates, provided it is spent. But when the government and the department sent out the information that for the purposes of a certain public work, $175,000 is to be appropriated, thus getting the advertising effect of that announcement, and then spend only $85,000, holding back $90,000 and handing it to us again the next year, we think they are very much in the position of an old gentleman up in my native township who used to give his son a penny to go to bed without his supper, and when the poor little fellow was sleeping the old man stole the penny and gave it to him again the next night. Now, I admit that this administration is an excellent advertising institution, and I want them to get full credit for everything they do. But I wish to state this: that every school child in the town of 
Goderich knows that this government took the advertising effect of $175,000 last year but spent only $85,000. In fact, Mr. Chairman, if you take the revotes of the last four years the total almost equals the $205,000 which we are getting this year. The minister explained1 to the deputation that he had his troubles, that as the estimates were late in going through it necessitated some delay in getting the work started. I should think that with unfinished contracts, and with a government who have a large submissive majority at its back, there should be no difficulty in the administration carrying out any work they wisned to undertake. Any contractor should know that.
Now I wish to place a few things on Hansard. I do not propose to be taking this matter up every year if I am longer in the house, but I do wish to make a brief review of Goderich harbour as presented to me by friends of this government, and which they wish to have presented to the Minister of Public Works. In 1896 Mr. Cameron, who had represented since confederation the constituency in which the town of Goderich is located, made the statement that in 1870 at his request Sir John A. Macdonald had appointed a commission to take evidence and to view the situation right along the coast line from Sarnia to 1 obermory. That commission reported that Goderich was the only harbour of refuge along that stretch of 150 or 200 miles, and feir John Macdonald's administration, at the request of a Liberal member representing that riding, took action in the matter. Sir John showed him every courtesy, without striving to make Mr. Cameron believe that because he was of a different political persuasion he should come hat in hand and on bended knee before the throne of the Minister of Public W orks. .Yet the other day, when I rose in the house to ask that another town in my constituency be given a public building, the answer of the Minister of Public Works was in effect that I had a nerve to ask for anything else in my constituency in view of the expenditures that had been made on this great national port, which was founded by the party to which I belong and which has been maintained by every government up to the present moment, despite the fact that in nearly every instance the sitting member has been politically opposed to the administration of the day.
The Hon. James Sutherland, Minister of Public Works in 1903, stated1 that up to that time Canada had spent $713,341.43 on the harbour. Before I proceed I wish to point out to hon. members of this house that this

Supply-Public Works-Bridges
is no ordinary harbour seeking a little donation. Through the activities of this harbour the Canadian National Railways, our own system, takes in over $1,000,000 of revenue in freight annually while the Canadian Pacific Railway takes in over three-quarters of a million. We bad afloat in the harbour last year 22 vessels carrying five and three-quarter million bushels of wheat. Last year twenty million bushels of wheat were handled at this port. In cargo deliveries to Canadian ports Goderich stood third, exceeded only by Port Col'bome and Montreal. In cargo deliveries to lake Huron and Georgian bay ports Goderich stood first. It appears to me that t the Hon. James Sutherland, the former Minister of Public Works, had a very good grasp of the situation and he sounded somewhat of a prophetic note. According to Hansard, Mr. Kemp of Toronto arose and asked this question :
Does this constitute all that the people of Goderich demand from the Department of Public Works?
The then Minister of Public Works replied:
No,, demands have been made, not only from Goderich, but the whole of the district and from Toronto west, that a breakwater should be built at that port. I myself believe it is a matter of necessity, if we are to have the benefit we should have on lake Huron. At present mostly all the shipping goes up the American side of the lake because we have not any harbour of refuge on the Canadian side. There are in addition splendid facilities already erected there in the shape of an elevator and other improvements at the harbour. I am very much impressed with the representation that a great deal of the grain of the west might be taken care of here if we had the proper facilities. However, the discussion of that matter will come up more properly when I ask the house to consider an appropriation for the purpose of improving Goderich harbour.
I should like the minister and the house to note this particularly:
I do not think it is a local work, but national in its nature. And the shipments to Canadian ports depend a great deal on our being able to take care of the grain which comes to these lake ports. Larger vessels could come to Goderich than to many of the other places. 1 am informed by the Grand Trunk that they would be prepared to take care of the grain, and that perhaps from fifteen to twenty millions of bushels could be easily handled if there was a very moderate expenditure on the harbour.
This was in 1903, and twenty-six years later -a quarter of a century-I am glad to be able to rise in this house and say that the prophetic utterance of the Hon. James Sutherland, a Liberal Minister of Public Works, has come true, and that in the past year there have been twenty million bushels. Mr. Maclaren, who represented North Perth at the time, said:
I have many communications from that part of the country with regard to the harbour, 3nd they say that for two hundred miles along the shore of lake Huron there is not a safe harbour for steamers to enter in case of storm, the grain men and millers all through that part of the country are very anxious to have the harbour put into proper shape. I may say also that I have a resolution passed by the Board of Trade of Stratford, and letter and telegrams from Mitchell, Seaforth, Goderich and all along the line; and I think the government should do something to put the harbor in proper shape. So far as I am concerned, I will do everything in my power.
I do not wish to go into any historical review of the situation by taking up the Hansards of the various years since confederation, but it has been freely admitted by every Minister of Public Works that Goderich is a harbour of national importance. Once more I would impress upon the minister the fact that any harbour which will contribute $1,000,000 in freight rates to the Canadian National Railways and three quarters of a million to the Canadian Pacific Railway is a harbour that should receive every consideration. On the strength of the sympathetic attitude of the present administration the Goderich Elevator Company has gone ahead with an expenditure this year, there being in course of erection a one million bushel extension to their elevator, at a cost of $350,000; and they confidently anticipate that the work will be proceeded with vigorously.
If we are going to have sessions of parliament lasting away on into midsummer, with estimates being brought down only at the close of the session, then we are going to-have a perpetual excuse for holding up a work of such importance nationally; and if that be the case I would appeal to the Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Mackenzie King) to call this house in session earlier in the year, say in the month of November, and let us get home by Easter. This would give the public works of Canada a chance. It is not the fault of hon. members on this side of the house that these estimates are going through at this late hour. I believe there are some unfinished contracts in connection with these public works, and while we are satisfied with the amount of $205,000 we believe all that money should be spent. We feel that it should be more; we feel that this government as well as previous governments has not kept pace with the activity of that harbour, but at all events we desire to get away from this business of putting $175,000 in the estimates and then spending less than half that amount.
I want to leave that thought with the government; I know the Minister of Public Works feels his responsibility, and I would appeal to the government to get away from petty

Supply-Public Works-Bridges
politics. They should not go into constituencies during 'by-elections-I am not speaking of my own riding in particular; -this has reference to the constituency of Victoria and others-and try to bribe the people of Canada with their own money. We believe that this is the money of the people of Canada which will be spent for the development of Goderich harbour. If it is to be a personal donation from this government I would suggest that the minister dress up as Santa Claus, get a few reindeers, have the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who knows the blue water highway well, drive him there and present the gift, if it is a national necessity it should be proceeded with vigorously, but if it is not a necessity not one dollar should be spent. Grain Traffic Through Goderich
Annually we handle from fifteen to twenty million bushels of grain from vessels to cars, IMr. Spotton.]
principally of Canadian origin, shipped from Fort William and Port Arthur. The major portion of this grain is destined for domestic milling and feeding requirements in Ontario and Quebec, with the balance going for export abroad through our Canadian eastern seaboard ports, and for domestic distribution in New England states. In 1929 we have handled through the "transit" elevators 17,000,000 bushels of Canadian and American grain, while an additional 4,000,000 bushels has been handled through the elevator of the Western Canada Flour Mills. The freight revenue on this will amount to over $1,800,000 of which our Canadian National Railways secures over 60 per cent. Additional to the grain traffic from our harbour is that of salt, coal, timber and other merchandise.
The first grain elevator at Goderich was built in 1860 by the Buffalo and Lake Huron . Railway, as a utility for handling grain from Milwaukee and Chicago for furtherance to New England points by the Buffalo gateway.
In 1890 it was converted into a facility for handling Canadian western grain from vessels to ears, for distribution to Ontario millers. In 1898 a company consisting largely of Ontario millers built a more modern structure of 500,000 bushels capacity, replaced in 1906 with one of concrete. The extension of the Canadian Pacific to Goderich in 1907 increased the field for domestic distribution, which necessitated the addition of another 500,000 bushel storage.
In 1923 this was doubled to 2,000,000 storage capacity, and now in 1929 the capacity is being increased another 1,000,000 bushels, and the mechanical equipment being enlarged and speeded up to make this elevator second to none on the lakes. Similarly the flour milling industry has grown at Goderich, and with it the manufacture of coarse and table salt. A mill of Ogilvies and Hutchinson which in 1875 served the local community and ground out probably 100 barrels a day, now the Western Canada Flour Mills, works to a maximum capacity of 2,300 barrels of flour and fifty tons of salt per day, every day in the year but Sunday.
That Goderich still stands to the fore in the handling of Canadian grain shipments through lake and bay ports is evidenced in the statement published by the Lake Shippers Clearance Association, Fort William, for the year ending July 31st., 1928, copy of which is herewith attached. This, of course, is exclusive of American grain. You will observe that with the exception of Port Colborne and Montreal, which are principally export points, Goderich exceeded Port McNicoll, Midland, Tiffin, Depot Harbour, Owen Sound and Sarnia.
Goderich, in the earlier schooner days, was established as a harbour of refuge, but in 1880 when steam carriers were supplanting the slower sailing vessel, the safety of this port for the larger craft was no more. Shallow draft in the harbour and an unprotected entrance made the mariner shun the place in stress of weather. Fortunately our governments realized the possibilities of the port and after private enterprise had demonstrated a determination to develop grain distribution and flour milling it was found necessary to build breakwaters and deepen the channels and harbour basin. But our Public Works departments have not kept pace with the development of traffic, especially in the accommodation of winter storage cargoes.

Last fall some twenty-two steamers held cargo for winter unloading, utilizing every available foot of space, and when this was filled other consignments had to proceed to Buffalo, Toledo, Erie and Fairport, where American railways secured the haulage on their export cargoes. Most of these storage vessels are American owned, which seek winter mooring at lake Huron ports so that they may make an early start in spring, to lake Michigan ports or to the westerly coal ports of lake Erie before Buffalo may be freed of ice. They find their winter mooring charges and shifting much cheaper at lake Huron ports than obtains along the expensive frontage of_ American ports. That the almost land-locked harbour of Goderich is secure is evidenced from the results of the gale of March 7th of this year, which shifted many and sank one or two steamers at lake Erie ports, to say nothing of the damages to wharves and bridges, while at Goderich every steamer remained secure.
While these twenty-two steamers of varying capacities held five and three quarter million bushels of grain last winter, there is ample area, if properly developed, for from thirty to thirty-five steamers of larger capacities which would easily accommodate twelve million bushels. The rail haulage on this grain would serve to keep our railways quite occupied throughout otherwise lean months, and similarly distribute valued wages to a number of men when they most require it. To attain this it is necessary that our Government prosecute promptly and expeditiously the program of improvement which has been requested of the Department of Public Works.

I want to make an appeal to the minister in connection with a portion of estimate No. 142 in regard to the interprovincial bridge over the Ottawa river at Hawkesbury, for which bridge an item of $40,000 has been in the estimates for a good many years. The proposal of the government is to build this bridge, provided the Quebec and Ontario governments will each contribute one-third of the cost. The difficulty of the position is that three governments are interested in this matter, and someone has to take the initiative. In all courtesy to the Minister of Public Works, I say that in his position he is the natural person to take this matter up with the other governments. I want to urge upon him that he ask the representatives of the other governments to meet him, talk the matter over and see if there is not some way whereby this very important and necessary work may be built. I want to ask him as a personal favour to take the matter up with the other governments and see if some solution cannot be found. Perhaps the minister does not know the location. The bridge is very urgently required, because there is no bridge over the Ottawa river between Ottawa and Ste. Annes, a distance of 110 miles or thereabouts. I know that at or near Hawkesbury and Grenville many lives have been lost in the last twenty years owing to the fact that people had to cross the river in the fall or spring of the year when the ice was bad and perhaps unwisely took the chance of crossing on bad ice. For humanitarian reasons, therefore, this bridge is very much needed and we have been agitating for it for a long time. With the present development of motor traffic there is a great necessity from the commercial point of view for the building of this bridge, because, if motorists coming from the United States were able to cross at Hawkesbury they would get into the north country via the shortest possible route instead of having to go to Montreal and taking a roundabout route. In the north country back of Grenville there are many lakes and wonderful scenery to attract people from the United States, and if this bridge were built it would be greatly used by motorists who desire to visit that section.
When the Borden government was in power, at my request it was decided to build the bridge and in 1914 tenders were called for the purpose. Unfortunately they came in just about the time war was declared, and on account of the war it was considered impossible to go on with any public works that were not absolutely necessary, so that no tender was accepted. As a matter of fact if the war 
had not intervened, this bridge would have been commenced in 1914 and completed many years ago. At that time it was the intention of the Dominion government to pay one-half the cost of the bridge, and on that basis arrangements were made with the provincial governments each to pay one-quarter. The minister tells me that the policy of the present government is to pay only one-third of the cost of bridges such as this, and he absolutely refuses to alter that decision. There should be a conference between the authorities of the Dominion and the two provinces on this particular point and with regard to this very necessary work. The counties on either side, one of which I have the honour to represent and the other 'being the county of Prescott in Ontario, have very little money spent in them. We are satisfied to have our friends from the great lakes and other parts of Canada receive the greater part of the public money that is being spent 'by the minister's department. We do however demand that this small expenditure be made, and surely in all fairness the people of those two counties ought to be helped to have this bridge built which is so very necessary for the preservation of life and also for the use of tourists who bring so much money into the country. Therefore I appeal to the minister to take a personal interest in the matter and to try to get the representatives of the provinces together to find a solution so that this bridge may be built in the near future.

This is a matter that has been before the government for some time and in regard to which the attitude of the government, as my hon. friend said, is quite well known. It is true that in the earlier years, as I am able to read the history of interprovincial bridges, it was clearly intended at the time of the passing of the British North America Act that bridges between provinces other than military bridges should be constructed by the two adjoining provinces. Practically the same rule applies as between counties. I am able to speak of the province of Ontario especially, and that rule applies as between two counties. Between townships, the two townships would build it, and between a township and a village the cost would be borne half by each. That has been the practice. Following out that, you would naturally expect that bridges that were not originally military bridges would be built by two adjoining provinces on an equal basis. However, the system has grown up under which the Dominion has contributed different proportions of the cost of bridges at different times, but for the last fifteen years the policy has .been consistent.

With that in view, the province of British Columbia has agreed to contribute a very substantial sum of .money towards that bridge. The Canadian Pacific Railway has agreed to contribute a very substantial sum of money towards that bridge. The city of Vancouver was quite prepared to contribute the major portion required for its erection, but it did request the Dominion government to make a contribution inasmuch as the bridge crosses a public harbour. Now the principle has been recognized of contributions towards interprovincial bridges; the principle was recognized by statute sixteen years ago of contributions towards bridges crossing public harbours, and the principle is' recognized of contributions towards international bridges. And I would point out that an enormous amount of international traffic crosses the bridges over Vancouver harbour. Recently, and after this government's refusal to make a contribution, a by-law was submitted to the electors of Vancouver for the construction of this bridge, involving payment by the city of 78594-194
Vancouver of the total cost with the exception of the contributions by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the provincial government. Since the defeat of the by-law I have received numerous letters on this subject from public bodies and others, which indicate to me the certainty that the bridge must be built, for the city is suffering in the meantime to a great extent through want of it. In view of these facts is the minister prepared to do what he has done-and I am not criticising him for having done it-in connection with the interprovincial bridge at Hawkesbury? In this case, apparently, the government is prepared to take the initiative; but I would point out that in the matter of the bridge which I am discussing the initiative has been taken by the province of British Columbia and the city of Vancouver. When the committee rose at six o'clock we were discussing the question of a bridge over the harbour at Vancouver and I undertook to advise the minister of the statute which authorized the subsidy. So the principle of granting subsidies for these bridges has been recognized for twenty-one years. In view of the fact that this subsidy was authorized for one bridge over a portion of Vancouver harbour but was never used; in view of the fact that the bridge Which was then contemplated has been built; in view of the fact that every cent which may be advanced by the Vancouver harbour commission will be repaid with interest out of the earnings of the bridge; in view of the further fact that the bridge which is now contemplated and for which this grant was asked is a rail bridge in addition to being a bridge for general purposes over the public harbour, I consider there is very much more merit to this request than to any of the requests I have heard for bridges over rivers or between provinces, and I would like to ask the minister again to take this matter under consideration and recommend this grant to the government.
